title: TARE
tagline: Measures what a Uniswap v4 hook really takes from your swap. 125,072 measurements, each replayable.
description:
When you swap on Uniswap v4, a small program called a hook runs during your trade, and it can
take a cut. Nobody publishes how much.

Uniswap asks hooks to declare it through the HookSwap and HookFee events its own guide
recommends. Across 1,559 hooks seen in 200,000 Base blocks, nine emit either one. The official
registry describes 978 entries with 27 fields each, 19 of them booleans — and not one of the 27
is a quantity. Its schema does not merely omit a number, it forbids adding one.

So TARE measures it. The obvious comparison is impossible: a v4 pool's identity — its PoolKey —
contains the hook's address, so "the same pool without its hook" does not exist. TARE does not
change the pool: it changes the hook. On a fork pinned to a block, anvil_setCode replaces the
hook's bytecode with an inert 89-byte stub. The poolId, the liquidity, slot0 and the reserves
stay byte-identical; the only thing that changed is the code that runs during the swap. Quote
the same swap twice and the gap IS what the hook took.

125,072 measurements, 7,817 pools, 112 hooks, 8 sizes, both directions. Every row carries its
block, its size, its direction, its label and a command that reproduces it. What could not be
measured keeps its reason instead of a zero: 61,916 of those rows are not values, and we
publish that too.
how_its_made:
The engine is Python. It pins an anvil fork of Base at block 50,614,000, quotes a swap through
V4Quoter, rewrites the hook's bytecode with anvil_setCode to an inert 89-byte stub that
satisfies Hooks.sol's return-data validation (96 bytes from beforeSwap, 64 otherwise, selector
echoed), quotes the same swap again, and restores the bytecode. The gap is the take. A gate
re-executes real swaps and checks the quote against the execution: 96.74 bps quoted, 96.74 bps
executed, to the wei.

The agent exposes fourteen named tools in three families — collection, analysis, action — and
the rule it cannot get around is written into the tool descriptions themselves: it never states
a number a tool did not return. Four of them are served over MCP to Claude Desktop, offline,
reading the committed corpus from disk.

Hedera carries the paid path: a fresh measurement costs 0.001 USDC over x402, settled through
the Blocky402 facilitator on Hedera testnet and read back on the mirror node — a settlement is
only counted if the mirror node returns it, never on our own word. The agent's identity is
HCS-14, derived from six canonical fields so a caller recomputes it instead of trusting us, and
the usage log is anchored on an HCS topic.

Ledger secures what is irreversible. The signing key lives in the Key Ring (wallet-cli ring),
and the guard's verdict is encoded as EIP-712 and rendered field by field on the device — you
do not sign an opaque digest. Cancelling returns 4001 and no call goes out.

The front end is React with no runtime backend: the whole corpus is column-encoded into 8.3 MB
and shipped inside the page, so the site answers with zero network requests. A browser
extension does the same offline, 12 kB of content script, and reads the Universal Router
calldata three seconds before you sign. When a cheaper door exists it builds the replacement
transaction and signs it through Permit2 (command list 0x0a10, PERMIT2_PERMIT then V4_SWAP) —
and never broadcasts it. On 99.71% of corpus rows there is no cheaper door, and it says so
rather than inventing one.

1,230 tests green across engine, API, MCP, guard, keyring and front end.
